chapter.name: Atoms
chapter.blurb: The chapter traces the structure of the atom from Thomson's model through the alpha-particle scattering experiment to Rutherford's nuclear model, and shows why a classical nuclear atom should be unstable and should not give line spectra. It then presents Bohr's three postulates for the hydrogen atom, the quantised orbits and energy levels they lead to, and the emission and absorption lines that arise from transitions between the levels. It ends with de Broglie's standing-wave explanation of the quantisation of angular momentum and the limitations of Bohr's model.

Describe the Geiger-Marsden alpha-particle scattering experiment (source, lead-brick collimation, thin gold foil, rotatable zinc sulphide screen and microscope) and state its observations (most pass through; about 0.14% scatter by more than 1 degree; about 1 in 8000 deflect by more than 90 degrees)

concepts.name: Models of the atom and the alpha-particle scattering experiment
concepts.description: Thomson's model, the Geiger-Marsden experiment and its observations, and Rutherford's nuclear model with the sizes of atom and nucleus.
concepts.idea: Because a few alpha-particles are turned back by a thin gold foil while most pass straight through, the positive charge and most of the mass of an atom must sit in a tiny nucleus, with the rest of the atom mostly empty space.
concepts.rule: Thomson's model: the positive charge is spread uniformly through the volume of the atom with electrons embedded in it. Geiger-Marsden experiment: alpha-particles from a radioactive source, collimated by lead bricks, fall on a thin gold foil; scattered particles give flashes on a rotatable zinc sulphide screen viewed through a microscope. Many alpha-particles pass through; only about 0.14% scatter by more than 1 degree and about 1 in 8000 deflect by more than 90 degrees. A backward deflection needs a large repulsive force, so the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a nucleus of size about 10^-15 m to 10^-14 m, while the atom is about 10^-10 m across (10,000 to 100,000 times larger). The light electrons do not appreciably affect the alpha-particles; the thin foil gives single scattering and the heavy gold nucleus (about 50 times the alpha-particle's mass) stays stationary.
concepts.example: If an atom of size 10^-10 m were enlarged to a field 100 m across, a nucleus of size 10^-14 m would be only 1 cm across.

If the solar system had the same proportions as the atom, find the radius the earth's orbit would have, compare it with the actual radius, and state what this shows about the atom.
questions.a: Ratio of orbit radius to nuclear radius = (10^-10)/(10^-15) = 10^5. With the same proportion the earth's orbit would have radius 10^5 x 7 x 10^8 m = 7 x 10^13 m. This is (7 x 10^13)/(1.5 x 10^11) = about 470 times, i.e. more than 100 times, the actual radius, so the earth would be much farther from the sun. Hence an atom contains a much greater fraction of empty space than the solar system does.
s: Ratio of electron-orbit radius to nuclear radius = 10^5
Scaled orbit radius = 10^5 x 7 x 10^8 m = 7 x 10^13 m, more than 100 times (about 470 times) the actual 1.5 x 10^11 m

questions.a: No. To turn an alpha-particle backwards a large repulsive force is needed, and that is possible only if the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated tightly in a small region so that the alpha-particle can come very close to all of it. In Thomson's model the positive charge is spread uniformly through the whole volume of the atom, so no such large force acts and backward scattering is not expected.
s: Backward deflection needs a large repulsive force from positive charge and mass concentrated at the centre

questions.q: The scattering data of Geiger and Marsden are analysed by computing the path of an alpha-particle scattered by a single stationary nucleus. Analyse the three assumptions or laws that make this treatment valid, giving the reason for each.
questions.a: (1) Single scattering: the gold foil is very thin (about 2.1 x 10^-7 m), so an alpha-particle suffers not more than one scattering while passing through it; the path due to one nucleus is therefore enough. (2) Stationary nucleus: the gold nucleus is about 50 times heavier than the alpha-particle, so it can be taken to stay at rest throughout. (3) The path is then computed from Newton's second law of motion with Coulomb's law for the electrostatic repulsion between the alpha-particle (charge 2e) and the nucleus (charge Ze).
s: Thin foil, so not more than one scattering per alpha-particle
Gold nucleus about 50 times heavier, so it stays stationary
Trajectory from Newton's second law with the Coulomb repulsion between charges 2e and Ze

questions.q: A student proposes to repeat the alpha-particle scattering experiment with a thin sheet of solid hydrogen in place of the gold foil and expects to see alpha-particles bouncing back just as with gold. Evaluate this expectation.
questions.a: The expectation is not sound. A hydrogen nucleus is much lighter than an alpha-particle (the alpha-particle has the mass of a helium atom), whereas the gold nucleus is about 50 times heavier than it. A heavy projectile cannot be turned back by a lighter target that itself recoils, so large-angle (backward) scattering would not be observed with hydrogen.
s: Judgement - backward scattering would not be seen with hydrogen
Reason - the hydrogen nucleus is lighter than the alpha-particle and recoils, unlike the heavy gold nucleus

Detector and record: a zinc sulphide screen with a microscope is mounted so that it can be rotated around the foil; each alpha-particle striking the screen gives a flash of light, and the number of flashes in a fixed time is counted at each scattering angle to obtain the number of scattered particles as a function of angle.
s: Radioactive alpha source collimated into a narrow beam by lead bricks
Thin gold foil as target, apparatus in vacuum
Rotatable zinc sulphide screen and microscope; count flashes at each scattering angle in a fixed time

concepts.name: Alpha-particle trajectory, impact parameter and distance of closest approach
concepts.description: The Coulomb force on an alpha-particle near a nucleus, how the impact parameter fixes the scattering angle, and the distance of closest approach from energy conservation.
concepts.idea: How strongly an alpha-particle is deflected depends on how nearly head-on it approaches the nucleus, and in a head-on approach it stops where all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy.
concepts.rule: The repulsive force between an alpha-particle (charge 2e) and a nucleus (charge Ze) at separation r is F = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) (2e)(Ze)/r^2, along the line joining them. The impact parameter b is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector from the centre of the nucleus: small b gives large scattering, a head-on collision (minimum b) makes the particle rebound (angle near 180 degrees), and large b gives almost no deflection. In a head-on approach energy conservation K = (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) (2e)(Ze)/d gives the distance of closest approach d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon0 K). The particle turns back without touching the nucleus, so d is an upper limit to the nuclear size.
concepts.example: For a 7.7 MeV alpha-particle aimed head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79), d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon0 K) is about 3.0 x 10^-14 m, that is 30 fm.

s: Approach - force increases as r decreases, kinetic energy decreases to zero (becoming potential energy)

questions.q: Alpha-particle P of kinetic energy 3.6 MeV is aimed head-on at a nucleus with Z = 30. Alpha-particle Q of kinetic energy 7.2 MeV is aimed head-on at a nucleus with Z = 90. Q has twice the energy, which alone would halve d, but its target has three times the charge, which triples d, so d for Q is 3/2 times that for P.
s: d for P = 24 fm
d for Q = 36 fm
P gets closer, because d is proportional to Z/K and Z/K is larger for Q

s: Judgement - 40 fm is only an upper limit, not the radius

questions.q: Devise a method that uses alpha-particles to set an upper limit on the size of the nucleus of a metal of known atomic number Z. State what must be known, the relation you would use, and how the limit could be made tighter.
questions.a: Send alpha-particles of known kinetic energy K at a thin foil of the metal and use those that rebound backwards, which have made nearly head-on collisions. For such a particle all the kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy at the turning point, so K = (1/(4 pi epsilon0))(2e)(Ze)/d, giving d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon0 K). Since the alpha-particle turned back without touching the nucleus, the nuclear radius is less than d. Because d is inversely proportional to K, alpha-particles of higher kinetic energy come closer and give a smaller, tighter upper limit.
s: Use head-on (backward-scattered) alpha-particles of known kinetic energy K and known Z
Relation d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon0 K) from energy conservation; nuclear radius is less than d
Tighter limit by using alpha-particles of higher kinetic energy, since d is proportional to 1/K

concepts.name: Electron orbits: kinetic, potential and total energy in the nuclear atom
concepts.description: The force condition for a circular electron orbit in hydrogen and the resulting kinetic energy, electrostatic potential energy and total energy in terms of the orbit radius.
concepts.idea: The electrostatic attraction of the nucleus supplies the centripetal force on the orbiting electron, and this fixes its kinetic, potential and total energies for a given orbit radius; the total energy is negative because the electron is bound.
concepts.rule: For a stable circular orbit in hydrogen, (1/(4 pi epsilon0)) e^2/r^2 = m v^2/r, so r = e^2/(4 pi epsilon0 m v^2). Kinetic energy K = e^2/(8 pi epsilon0 r); electrostatic potential energy U = -e^2/(4 pi epsilon0 r); total energy E = K + U = -e^2/(8 pi epsilon0 r). Hence K = -E and U = 2E. E is negative for a bound electron; if E were positive the electron would not follow a closed orbit.
concepts.example: With e^2/(4 pi epsilon0) = 1.44 eV nm, an orbit of radius 0.24 nm has U = -6 eV, K = 3 eV and total energy E = -3 eV.

concepts.idea: Each element gives its own set of discrete spectral lines, but a classical orbiting electron would radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus, so Rutherford's model can explain neither the stability of atoms nor their line spectra.
concepts.rule: Condensed matter and dense gases emit a continuous spectrum; a rarefied gas excited at low pressure emits only certain wavelengths, giving an emission line spectrum of bright lines on a dark background that is characteristic of the element. White light passed through the gas shows dark lines at precisely the same wavelengths: the absorption spectrum. Classically, a revolving electron is accelerated and so radiates electromagnetic waves, loses energy and spirals into the nucleus; the frequency of the emitted waves equals the frequency of revolution v/(2 pi r), which would change continuously and give a continuous spectrum. Both predictions contradict observation.

concepts.name: Bohr's postulates and the orbits of the hydrogen atom
concepts.description: Bohr's three postulates, the quantisation of angular momentum, and how the radius, speed and angular momentum of the allowed orbits depend on n.
concepts.idea: Bohr kept Rutherford's orbits but allowed only those in which the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/(2 pi); in these the electron does not radiate, and light is emitted only in jumps between them.
concepts.rule: (i) The electron can revolve in certain stable orbits (stationary states of definite total energy) without emitting radiant energy. (ii) The allowed orbits are those with angular momentum L = n h/(2 pi), n = 1, 2, 3, ... (iii) In a transition to an orbit of lower energy a photon is emitted with h nu = E_i - E_f. The radius of the nth orbit is r_n = (n^2/m)(h/(2 pi))^2 (4 pi epsilon0/e^2), proportional to n^2, with r_1 = 5.3 x 10^-11 m (the Bohr radius). From m v r = n h/(2 pi), the speed is proportional to 1/n.
concepts.example: For n = 10 the orbit radius is 100 times the Bohr radius, the angular momentum is 10 h/(2 pi) and the speed is one-tenth of the speed in the first orbit.

concepts.rule: E_n = -m e^4/(8 n^2 epsilon0^2 h^2) = -2.18 x 10^-18/n^2 J = -13.6/n^2 eV. n = 1 is the ground state (-13.6 eV); n = 2, 3, ... are excited states (-3.40 eV, -1.51 eV, -0.85 eV, ...); n = infinity is at 0 eV, above which the electron is free. Ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV; from level n it is 13.6/n^2 eV. In a transition from n_i to a lower n_f a photon of frequency given by h nu = E_ni - E_nf is emitted; a photon of exactly this energy can be absorbed in the reverse transition, giving dark absorption lines.
concepts.example: E_6 - E_3 = -0.38 eV - (-1.51 eV) = 1.13 eV is the energy of the photon emitted when the electron drops from n = 6 to n = 3.

concepts.name: De Broglie's explanation of quantised orbits and the limitations of Bohr's model
concepts.description: The electron as a standing particle wave on its orbit, leading to Bohr's angular momentum condition, and the two stated limitations of Bohr's model.
concepts.idea: An electron orbit is allowed only if a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths fits round it, which is exactly Bohr's angular momentum condition; even so, the model works only for single-electron atoms and says nothing about line intensities.
concepts.rule: Standing-wave condition: 2 pi r_n = n lambda, n = 1, 2, 3, ... With lambda = h/p = h/(m v_n) this gives m v_n r_n = n h/(2 pi). Limitations: (i) the model applies only to hydrogenic atoms (a nucleus of charge +Ze with a single electron, such as hydrogen, singly ionised helium and doubly ionised lithium) and cannot be extended even to helium, because it omits the forces between electrons; (ii) it cannot explain the relative intensities of the spectral lines. Complex atoms need quantum mechanics.
concepts.example: For n = 4, four de Broglie wavelengths fit into the circumference of the orbit: 2 pi r_4 = 4 lambda.

questions.q: Write a short reasoned note for a classmate explaining why Bohr's method cannot simply be reused for the helium atom, what feature of that atom the model leaves out, and what kind of theory is needed instead.
questions.a: Bohr's model is formulated with only one electrical force, that between the positively charged nucleus and a single electron, so it applies to hydrogenic atoms. A helium atom has two electrons, and each electron interacts not only with the nucleus but also with the other electron. These electron-electron forces, which necessarily appear in multi-electron atoms, are not included in the model, and attempts to analyse such atoms on Bohr's lines did not succeed. For complex atoms a new theory based on quantum mechanics has to be used, which gives a more complete picture of atomic structure.
s: Bohr's model includes only the nucleus-electron force, valid for single-electron (hydrogenic) atoms
Helium has electron-electron forces, which the model leaves out
A theory based on quantum mechanics is needed for complex atoms
